items.definition: To have an influence on something or someone; often confused with the noun effect.
items.etymology: From Latin affectus, past participle of afficere 'to act on', from ad 'to' and facere 'to do'.
items.example_sentence: Lack of sleep can affect your judgement more than you notice.

items.definition: A result or change produced by a cause; as a verb it means to bring about.
items.etymology: From Latin effectus 'accomplishment', from efficere 'to work out', from ex 'out' and facere 'to do'.
items.example_sentence: The new schedule had an immediate effect on morale.

items.definition: To suggest something without saying it directly; the speaker implies, the listener infers.
items.etymology: From Old French emplier 'to enfold', from Latin implicare 'to entwine'.
items.example_sentence: Her silence seemed to imply that she disagreed.

items.definition: To reach a conclusion from evidence or reasoning rather than from a direct statement.
items.etymology: From Latin inferre 'to bring in', from in 'in' and ferre 'to carry'.
items.example_sentence: From the empty parking lot, we inferred that the shop had closed early.

items.definition: To consist of or be made up of; the whole comprises the parts.
items.etymology: From French compris, past participle of comprendre 'to contain', from Latin comprehendere.
items.example_sentence: The committee comprises five scientists and two lawyers.

items.definition: To openly disregard a rule or convention; often confused with flaunt.
items.etymology: Possibly from Dutch fluiten 'to whistle, to hiss at'.
items.example_sentence: Drivers who flout the speed limit near schools face heavy fines.

items.definition: To display something conspicuously to attract admiration or envy.
items.etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in English in the sixteenth century.
items.example_sentence: He liked to flaunt his new watch at every meeting.

items.definition: Feeling sick to the stomach; traditionally it meant causing nausea.
items.etymology: From Latin nauseosus, from nausea 'seasickness', from Greek naus 'ship'.
items.example_sentence: The winding mountain road made everyone in the back seat nauseous.

items.definition: Opposite to what was expected or intended, in a way that is pointed or amusing; not simply unlucky.
items.etymology: From Greek eironikos 'dissembling', from eiron 'one who feigns ignorance'.
items.example_sentence: It was ironic that the fire station burned down during a safety inspection.

items.definition: In the exact sense of the words, without exaggeration or metaphor.
items.etymology: From Late Latin litteralis 'of letters or writing', from littera 'letter'.
items.example_sentence: The old bridge literally shook every time a truck crossed it.

items.definition: To kill or destroy a large part of something; originally to kill one in every ten.
items.etymology: From Latin decimare, the Roman punishment of executing every tenth soldier, from decimus 'tenth'.
items.example_sentence: A late frost decimated the region's apple harvest.

items.definition: Great wickedness, or the extreme seriousness of something bad; often misused to mean large size.
items.etymology: From Latin enormitas, from enormis 'irregular, huge', from ex 'out of' and norma 'rule'.
items.example_sentence: Only years later did the public grasp the enormity of the fraud.

items.definition: So surprised or confused that one does not know how to react.
items.etymology: From Latin non plus 'no more', meaning a state in which nothing more can be said or done.
items.example_sentence: The interviewer was nonplussed when the candidate asked to reschedule mid-interview.

items.definition: Puzzled or bewildered; not the same as amused.
items.etymology: From be- 'thoroughly' and muse 'to ponder'.
items.example_sentence: She gave a bemused look at the instructions, which were printed upside down.

items.definition: Impartial and not influenced by personal advantage; distinct from uninterested.
items.etymology: From dis- 'not' and interested in the old sense 'having a stake in'.
items.example_sentence: A disinterested referee has no ties to either team.

items.definition: To read something thoroughly and carefully, though it is often used to mean skim.
items.etymology: Probably from per- 'thoroughly' and use, in late Middle English.
items.example_sentence: Peruse the contract before you sign it, every clause included.

items.definition: Last but one in a series; second to last, not the very last.
items.etymology: From Latin paenultimus, from paene 'almost' and ultimus 'last'.
items.example_sentence: The penultimate chapter sets up the twist in the final one.

items.definition: A remark that expresses praise or admiration.
items.etymology: From Italian complimento, from Spanish cumplimiento 'fulfilment of courtesy'.
items.example_sentence: Her thoughtful compliment on the design made the team's week.

items.definition: Something that completes or goes well with something else.
items.etymology: From Latin complementum, from complere 'to fill up'.
items.example_sentence: A crisp white wine is a good complement to grilled fish.

items.definition: A fundamental truth, rule or belief that guides behaviour or reasoning.
items.etymology: From Latin principium 'beginning, source', from princeps 'first'.
items.example_sentence: The design follows one principle: never lose the user's data.

items.definition: First in order of importance; main. As a noun it can mean the head of a school or a sum of money.
items.etymology: From Latin principalis 'first, chief', from princeps 'first'.
items.example_sentence: Cost was the principal reason the project was cancelled.

items.definition: Careful and tactful in what one says or does, so as to avoid embarrassment.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin discretus 'discerning', from discernere 'to separate'.
items.example_sentence: Please be discreet about the merger until it is announced.

items.definition: Separate and distinct; made of individual parts.
items.etymology: From Latin discretus 'separated', from discernere 'to separate'.
items.example_sentence: The course is split into discrete modules you can take in any order.

items.definition: To draw out a response, answer or fact from someone.
items.etymology: From Latin elicere 'to draw out by trickery', from ex 'out' and lacere 'to entice'.
items.example_sentence: The survey was designed to elicit honest feedback.

items.definition: Forbidden by law, rules or custom.
items.etymology: From Latin illicitus, from in 'not' and licitus 'allowed'.
items.example_sentence: Customs officers seized a shipment of illicit tobacco.

items.definition: To refer to something indirectly, without naming it explicitly.
items.etymology: From Latin alludere 'to play with', from ad 'towards' and ludere 'to play'.
items.example_sentence: The speech alluded to last year's layoffs without mentioning them.

items.definition: To escape or avoid someone or something, often cleverly; to fail to be grasped.
items.etymology: From Latin eludere 'to escape by trickery', from ex 'out' and ludere 'to play'.
items.example_sentence: The answer continued to elude the researchers for a decade.

items.definition: To make certain that something happens or is the case.
items.etymology: From Anglo-Norman enseurer, related to Old French aseurer 'to assure'.
items.example_sentence: Double-check the address to ensure the package arrives.

items.definition: To arrange for compensation in the event of loss or damage, usually through a policy.
items.etymology: A variant of ensure, specialised in the seventeenth century for financial protection.
items.example_sentence: They decided to insure the camera before the trip.

items.definition: Not moving or not intended to be moved.
items.etymology: From Latin stationarius 'belonging to a military station', from statio 'standing'.
items.example_sentence: The bus was stationary when the cyclist hit its mirror.

items.definition: Writing materials such as paper, envelopes and pens.
items.etymology: From stationer, a medieval bookseller with a fixed shop, from Latin stationarius.
items.example_sentence: The hotel left monogrammed stationery on the desk.

items.definition: Happening again and again, with breaks in between.
items.etymology: From Old French continuel, from Latin continuus 'uninterrupted'.
items.example_sentence: The continual interruptions made it hard to finish the report.

items.definition: Without any pause or interruption at all.
items.etymology: From Latin continuus 'uninterrupted', from continere 'to hang together'.
items.example_sentence: The factory runs on continuous power from two separate lines.

items.definition: At or to a greater physical distance; further is preferred for extent or degree.
items.etymology: A Middle English variant of further, influenced by far.
items.example_sentence: The trail goes farther into the canyon than the map shows.

items.definition: Deserving regret; unfortunate. A situation is regrettable, a person is regretful.
items.etymology: From regret, from Old French regreter 'to lament'.
items.example_sentence: The delay was regrettable but could not have been avoided.

items.definition: Able to be believed; convincing.
items.etymology: From Latin credibilis, from credere 'to believe'.
items.example_sentence: The witness gave a credible account of the accident.

items.definition: Too ready to believe things, especially on weak evidence.
items.etymology: From Latin credulus, from credere 'to believe'.
items.example_sentence: Scammers target credulous buyers with offers that are too good to be true.

items.definition: Full of twists and turns; excessively complex. Distinct from torturous.
items.etymology: From Latin tortuosus, from tortus 'a twisting'.
items.example_sentence: The bill took a tortuous path through three committees.

items.definition: Causing great pain or suffering.
items.etymology: From torture, from Latin tortura 'twisting'.
items.example_sentence: The final kilometre of the climb was torturous in the heat.

items.definition: To recommend or order a treatment, or to lay down a rule.
items.etymology: From Latin praescribere 'to write before', from prae 'before' and scribere 'to write'.
items.example_sentence: The doctor prescribed rest and plenty of fluids.

items.definition: To forbid something, especially by law; nearly the opposite of prescribe.
items.etymology: From Latin proscribere 'to publish in writing', the Roman practice of posting names of outlaws.
items.example_sentence: The new rules proscribe the use of phones during exams.

items.definition: Having a strong dislike of or opposition to something.
items.etymology: From Latin aversus 'turned away', from avertere.
items.example_sentence: Most investors are averse to losing money they cannot recover.

items.definition: Harmful or unfavourable.
items.etymology: From Latin adversus 'turned against', from advertere.
items.example_sentence: The trial recorded no serious adverse effects.

items.definition: Every other one in a series; or occurring by turns.
items.etymology: From Latin alternatus, from alternare 'to do by turns', from alter 'other'.
items.example_sentence: The pool is open to children on alternate Saturdays.

items.definition: One of two or more available possibilities.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin alternativus, from alternare 'to do by turns'.
items.example_sentence: If the bridge is closed, the ferry is the only alternative.

items.definition: To tell someone confidently that something is true, to remove their doubt.
items.etymology: From Old French aseurer, from Latin ad 'to' and securus 'safe'.
items.example_sentence: I can assure you the data is backed up every night.

items.definition: To leave one's own country to settle permanently in another.
items.etymology: From Latin emigrare, from ex 'out of' and migrare 'to move'.
items.example_sentence: Her grandparents emigrated from Ireland in the 1950s.

items.definition: To come to live permanently in a foreign country.
items.etymology: From Latin immigrare, from in 'into' and migrare 'to move'.
items.example_sentence: Many engineers immigrate to the city for its tech jobs.

items.definition: Famous and respected within a particular field.
items.etymology: From Latin eminere 'to stand out', from ex 'out' and minere 'to project'.
items.example_sentence: An eminent surgeon reviewed the case.

items.definition: About to happen very soon.
items.etymology: From Latin imminere 'to overhang, to threaten', from in 'upon' and minere 'to project'.
items.example_sentence: Dark clouds warned of an imminent storm.

items.definition: To come before something in time, order or position.
items.etymology: From Latin praecedere, from prae 'before' and cedere 'to go'.
items.example_sentence: A short welcome will precede the keynote.

items.definition: To begin or continue a course of action; to move forward.
items.etymology: From Latin procedere, from pro 'forward' and cedere 'to go'.
items.example_sentence: Once the form is signed, we can proceed with the order.

items.definition: Famous or important in history; historical means simply concerning the past.
items.etymology: From Greek historikos, from historia 'inquiry, narrative'.
items.example_sentence: The treaty was signed in a historic hall in Vienna.

items.definition: Relating to the past or to the study of history.
items.etymology: From Latin historicus, from Greek historikos 'of history'.
items.example_sentence: The museum holds historical records from the founding of the town.

items.definition: Relating to the economy or to economics; economical means thrifty.
items.etymology: From Greek oikonomikos 'skilled in household management', from oikos 'house'.
items.example_sentence: The report forecasts slower economic growth next year.

items.definition: Giving good value for the money or effort spent; thrifty.
items.etymology: From economic, from Greek oikonomia 'household management'.
items.example_sentence: A smaller car is more economical to run in the city.

items.definition: Open to debate; in American usage also of no practical relevance.
items.etymology: From Old English mot 'assembly', where matters were discussed.
items.example_sentence: Since the event was cancelled, the question of tickets is moot.

items.definition: To make a problem or injury worse; informally, to annoy.
items.etymology: From Latin aggravare 'to make heavy', from ad 'to' and gravis 'heavy'.
items.example_sentence: Running on the sprained ankle will only aggravate it.

items.definition: A false, distorted or absurd imitation of something serious.
items.etymology: From French travesti 'disguised', from Italian travestire 'to disguise'.
items.example_sentence: The rushed trial was a travesty of justice.

items.definition: Being the only one of its kind; strictly, it does not take degrees like very.
items.etymology: From French unique, from Latin unicus 'only, single', from unus 'one'.
items.example_sentence: Each snowflake's pattern is effectively unique.
